title: "Software engineering is not about writing code" — Benoit Schillings, Google DeepMind VP of Research

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is AI code generation, the Pitchfork project, and the future of software engineering, matching the inclusion criterion of code generation as the main research object. The talk centers on coding assistants throughout while extending to scientific research applications in chemistry and biology in the final section. The talk describes forward-looking research on a one-month to one-year horizon at Google DeepMind rather than deployed production systems. The keynote is accessible to AI engineers but covers deep concepts including self-play, inductive architecture, and open-ended evaluation methodology. This is a keynote presentation at the AI Engineer conference. All evidence anchors are sourced directly from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Benoit Schillings, VP of Research at Google DeepMind, leads the Thinking, Reasoning, and Coding teams tasked with developing technology to make Gemini exceptional within a one-month to one-year horizon. Previously at Google X, he worked on projects like Waymo and Glass. He recounts starting the Pitchfork project at X in 2018 to explore how ML could improve code writing, noting that Google colleagues initially dismissed the idea. He also admits dismissing vibe coding himself before being proven wrong. Schillings frames software history through three eras: the machine-constrained assembly era where extracting maximum performance was paramount; the cloud era where modular design and human cognitive limits (7-9 token context) shaped software processes; and the current AI frontier where writing code is no longer the bottleneck—ensuring correctness, architecture, and inductive thinking are. He declares syntax generation effectively solved, with the frontier now at multi-step codebase management (citing a 35 million line PHP codebase example) and architectural-level reasoning. Code is uniquely suited to ML due to abundant training data from GitHub and verifiability through compilation and unit tests. However, with approximately 80% of new GitHub code now machine-generated, human training data is saturating. The solution is self-play, analogous to Alpha Zero's superhuman performance achieved without human knowledge—models generate their own challenges, validate answers, and even judge architecture. Writing code is now nearly free, meaning code volume will explode and humans will stop reading generated code, paralleling how nobody checks compiler assembly output. This raises critical questions about guardrails, security, and teaching models to write correct code from the start. Evaluation benchmarks must evolve beyond simple run-and-verify tests like HumanEval toward open-ended problems such as text compression, where the loss function includes compressed file size plus source code size. Schillings argues that code writing is not merely a chain of tokens but a visual, spatial activity, and that Gemini's multimodal design enables models to think in dynamic representations. He raises the provocative idea of creating new programming languages specifically for models—strongly typed, inspired by Lean, carrying program-proof burdens, and not necessarily human-readable. Beyond code, rapid free experimentation will transform chemistry (where humans barely understand molecules beyond 20 atoms) and biology (where nature engineered brilliantly but documented poorly). He concludes with the concept of the gold we cannot see: human evolutionary bias limits our solution space, while ML offers a fundamentally different viewpoint to uncover breakthroughs hidden in plain sight.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Benoit Schillings introduces himself as VP of Research at Google DeepMind, leading teams developing technology for Gemini on a one-month to one-year horizon. He describes his prior experience at Google X on projects like Waymo and Glass, and his team's research scope spanning code, reasoning, topology, and reinforcement learning.

sections.title: The origin story of the Pitchfork project
sections.summary: Schillings recounts launching Pitchfork at X in 2018 to explore ML for code writing, initially dismissed by Google colleagues. He admits wrongly dismissing vibe coding. He reflects on his 45-year coding career from assembly to Python, illustrating how even experienced engineers resist change.

sections.title: Historical eras of software development
sections.summary: Three eras are outlined: machine-constrained assembly, cloud-era modular design limited by human cognitive capacity (7-9 token context), and the current AI frontier where code writing is no longer the bottleneck—ensuring correctness and architecture are. Humans retain edges in architecture and inductive thinking.

sections.title: Current state of AI code generation
sections.summary: Schillings declares superhuman syntax generation achieved. The real challenge is multi-step codebase management—navigating massive existing codebases like 35 million lines of PHP. Code is unique for ML due to abundant GitHub training data and verifiability through compilation and unit tests.

sections.title: Self-play and training data saturation
sections.summary: With 80% of new GitHub code machine-generated, human training data is saturating. The solution is self-play, analogous to Alpha Zero achieving superhuman performance without human data. Models can now create challenges, validate answers, and judge architecture, making compute the primary scaling factor.

sections.title: Changing economics of software engineering
sections.summary: Writing code is now nearly free, which will cause code volume to explode. Humans will stop reading generated code, paralleling how nobody checks compiler assembly output. This raises critical questions about design adequacy, system reliability, and new processes needed to manage the explosion.

sections.title: Guardrails and security
sections.summary: Vulnerability detection by models creates a never-ending cycle of finding and patching flaws. The harder goal is teaching models to write correct code from the start, which is very difficult due to context dependence. Schillings argues security implications deserve as much attention as code generation itself.

sections.title: Inductive architecture and model planning
sections.summary: Models still struggle with inductive architecture—transferring knowledge across domains and finding intersections between concepts. Teaching models correct planning and problem decomposition for complex software systems is identified as a critical needed skill for the next phase of AI coding.

sections.title: Evolution of evaluation benchmarks
sections.summary: Schillings critiques current benchmarks like HumanEval as too limited—they only verify code runs and produces correct output. He advocates for open-ended problems such as text compression, where models must write the best lossless compressor with a loss function combining compressed file size and source code size, forcing novel algorithmic discovery.

sections.title: Moving beyond chain-of-thought tokens
sections.summary: Code writing is a visual and spatial activity, not just a chain of tokens. Schillings explains that Gemini was designed as multimodal from the onset, with text as only one modality. Models must learn to think in spatial and dynamic representations to solve problems, which will become a must-have capability.

sections.title: New languages for models
sections.summary: Schillings proposes creating new programming languages designed specifically for models rather than humans. Since the pain of writing code no longer exists, languages could be strongly typed, inspired by Lean, carry program-proof burdens, and need not be human-readable—shifting correctness responsibility onto the model.

sections.title: Future applications in chemistry and biology
sections.summary: Rapid free experimentation through code will transform science. In chemistry, humans understand very little beyond 20-atom molecules, and 10,000 atoms approaches life-like complexity. In biology, nature engineered brilliantly but documented poorly—models can find elusive relationships. Schillings concludes with the concept of gold we cannot see: human evolutionary bias limits our solution space, while ML offers a different viewpoint to discover breakthroughs hidden in plain sight.
